newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl's CDU urges industry to create jobs.
newsitem.headline: Kohl's CDU urges industry to create jobs.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) criticised industry on Thursday for not taking advantage of regulatory changes that they said improved the conditions for investment and new jobs.

CDU general secretary Peter Hintze said in a statement that the government had enacted legislation that made it easier for small companies to hire and fire employees and that it was on the way to implementing deep tax cuts.
"These were demands made by the employers," he said. "Now the employers are called upon to do their part and create jobs."

The Federal Labour Office reported earlier that German unemployment rose again in February to 4.32 million, up 5,000 from January, on a seasonally adjusted basis. On an unadjusted basis, 4.67 million people were without jobs, or 12.2 percent.
Although the rise in unemployment slowed last month, it set another post-war record and continued to hover at levels not seen since the turbulent 1930s.
Getting control of the jobs crisis has become an urgent political task facing Kohl. It could become the issue that makes or breaks the government's re-election bid next year.
The impact on the deficit could also cause Bonn to fail the Maastricht treaty fiscal targets for Europe's single currency.
But as the latest jobless data were released, two leading Germany industry groups threw cold water on the idea that a significant number of new jobs would be created soon.

The Federation of German Chambers of Industry and Commerce (DIHT) disputed the government's forecast on economic growth this year, saying it saw just two percent not 2.5 percent as predicted in Bonn's annual economic report.
A DIHT survey of its members, which include the great majority of mid-sized companies, showed that few companies were planning to increase investment in Germany this year.

The Federation of German Industry (BDI), the main industrial lobby for German blue-chips, said companies would continue to invest abroad as the economy becomes more global and urged the government to improve conditions further at home.

"Compared to their competitors German companies have to battle with a series of competitive burdens," BDI said in a summary of its annual report. "Among these are the highest corporate taxes in the world."
But Hintze, responding to repeated statements by German industry and employers' groups, said bluntly that it was time for employers to create new jobs before making new demands.
"It is hardly helpful and also not very credible when individual voices from the employers' camp demand further action from the state before having anything to show for themselves," he said.
